subtype: Approach: building a small campaign team [Action]
passage: Tejas knew he could not reach every class alone. So he asked three friends from different classes: Nitin in 9B for posters, Shreya in 8A for class visits, and Imran in 10C for speeches. Every day at ten past one, in the corridor by the water cooler, the four met for ten minutes with three questions: what's done, what's stuck, who haven't we reached? On Tuesday Nitin's posters hung on every floor. On Wednesday Shreya said the Class 8s felt ignored, so Tejas added a visit. On Thursday Imran read a draft speech, and it got better after two edits. Nobody had a title. Each had a task and a time.

qa.q: Where did the four meet each day?
qa.a: They met in the corridor by the water cooler.

qa.q: What does Tejas's decision to add a visit suggest about how he feels toward the Class 8s?
qa.a: Tejas cares that the Class 8s feel included, and responds to Shreya's report with an action, not a defence.

qa.q: What could Tejas do if the ten-minute meeting shows a task is stuck, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could pair the stuck task with a second helper for one day, because sharing it lets the campaign keep moving without adding meetings.

qa.q: How might Shreya see the daily meeting?
qa.a: Shreya likely feels the voice of the Class 8s is heard, since a concern raised on Wednesday changed the plan.

grounding: The candidate recruits friends from different classes to handle posters, class visits and speeches, and meets daily for ten minutes to check progress and reach different groups of voters.

subtype: Approach: building a small campaign team [Action]

"I can't do this alone," Preeti said, spreading her election notes across Yamini's bed. "I know Class 10 because I'm in it. But who's going to talk to Class 7?"

"My cousin Divya's in Class 7," Yamini said. "She's loud. People listen to her."

"Perfect. Class visits for the juniors. What about posters?"

"Aftab from 9B draws really well."

"And someone for Class 12? They won't take a Class 10 kid seriously."

"Ask Harpreet didi from your bus. She likes you."

By Wednesday there were five of them. "Ten minutes every day at lunch, by the water tank," Preeti said. "Everyone says what they did yesterday and what's next. That's it."

On Friday Divya reported, "Class 7 wants more sports." Preeti wrote it down. "Then that's in the speech."

qa.q: Where did the team meet every day?
qa.a: They met by the water tank at lunch for ten minutes every day.

qa.q: Why did Preeti say "I can't do this alone"?
qa.a: Preeti felt worried and overwhelmed about reaching students in other classes she did not know well.

qa.q: What could Preeti try if the daily meetings began to drag?
qa.a: She could keep a small shared checklist so each person only reports on their own line, keeping the meeting to ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Divya see being part of the campaign team?
qa.a: Divya likely feels valued and excited, because her report about Class 7 wanting more sports went straight into the speech.

grounding: Shows a candidate recruiting helpers from different classes for posters, class visits and speeches, and holding short daily check-ins.

subtype: Approach: building a small campaign team [Action]
passage:
I'm Reena, and I thought running for house captain meant giving one good speech. My friend Dhruv laughed when I said that. "You'll talk to your own class. What about the other four hundred?"

So I built a team. Dhruv took posters, because he could draw. A girl from Class 8 who played basketball with me offered to visit junior classes. A Class 11 boy from my coding club helped me write a short speech. There were four of us.

We met for ten minutes every morning before assembly, on the steps outside the lab. Each person said what they'd done and what was blocked. Once the posters were torn down in one corridor; the next morning we'd already replaced them.

I lost narrowly. But juniors I'd never met told me they voted for me, and that surprised me more than anything.

qa.q: Where did the team meet every morning?
qa.a: They met on the steps outside the lab for ten minutes every morning before assembly.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when juniors said they had voted for Reena?
qa.a: Reena felt surprised and quietly touched, since those were students Reena had never met.

qa.q: What else could Reena's team have done to reach more voters?
qa.a: They could have asked each class what it most wanted and shaped a line of the speech for each group, not just visited them.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Reena's change of plan after his comment?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt pleased and respected, since Reena took his warning seriously and gave him the posters to run.

grounding: A reflective account of a candidate recruiting helpers from different classes for posters, visits and speeches, and meeting briefly each day to check progress.
